title: Sequence
body:
An infinite ordered list of numbers, $\{a_n\} = a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$, which is really just a
function whose input is restricted to the positive integers. Calc 2 cares about one question only:
**does it settle down?**

$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n = L
$$

means the terms get and stay arbitrarily close to $L$. If such an $L$ exists the sequence
**converges**, otherwise it **diverges**. This is [[Limit]] at infinity from [[CALCULUS 1]] with
the domain thinned out to the integers, and that thinning is why you may evaluate a sequence limit
by treating $n$ as a continuous variable: if $\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x) = L$ and $a_n = f(n)$, then
$a_n \to L$ too. The converse fails ($\sin(\pi n)$ is always $0$, $\sin(\pi x)$ oscillates
forever), which is worth remembering as the reason the implication only runs one way.

## Sequence versus series

**The single most confused pair in the course.** A [[Infinite Series|series]] is built out of a
sequence but is a different object:

| | Sequence | Series |
|---|---|---|
| is | a list $a_1, a_2, a_3,\dots$ | a sum $a_1 + a_2 + a_3 + \cdots$ |
| converges when | the terms approach a value | the **partial sums** approach a value |
| $a_n = 1/n$ | converges to $0$ | **diverges** (the harmonic series) |

Those last two cells are the whole point. The terms of the harmonic series go to zero and the sum
still runs off to infinity, which is why the $n$th term test in [[Convergence Tests]] can only ever
prove divergence.

## The standard limits

- $r^n \to 0$ if $|r| < 1$, $\to 1$ if $r = 1$, diverges otherwise. This is the geometric sequence
  and it is the backbone of [[Convergence Tests]]
- $n^{1/n} \to 1$ and $(1 + \tfrac{x}{n})^n \to e^x$
- $\frac{n^k}{c^n} \to 0$ for $c > 1$: **exponentials beat polynomials**, always. Same ordering
  [[Time Complexity]] uses for algorithms, and the same fact
- $\frac{c^n}{n!} \to 0$: factorials beat exponentials. This is why the ratio test finishes
  $\sum \frac{x^n}{n!}$ so quickly
- for indeterminate forms, take logs or use L'Hôpital on the continuous version

## Bounded and monotonic

$$
\text{monotonic} + \text{bounded} \Rightarrow \text{convergent}
$$

Monotonic means always non-increasing or always non-decreasing; bounded means the terms stay inside
some fixed interval. **This is an existence theorem: it proves a limit exists without telling you
what it is**, which is the same service the Intermediate Value Theorem does for roots in
[[CALCULUS 1]]. It is the standard way to handle a recursively defined sequence like
$a_{n+1} = \sqrt{2 + a_n}$, where induction gives you the bound and the monotonicity, and only then
does solving $L = \sqrt{2+L}$ become legal. Solving for $L$ first assumes the answer.

## Related

- [[Infinite Series]]: what you get when you add a sequence up
- [[Convergence Tests]]: every one of them is a statement about a sequence, usually the sequence of
  partial sums or of ratios
- [[Limit]] and [[Continuity]] in [[CALCULUS 1]]
- [[Proof By Induction]] in [[DISCRETE MATH]]: recursively defined sequences are proved bounded and
  monotonic by induction, and a recurrence is a sequence
- [[Recursion]] in [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]]: a recursive function generating
  successive approximations is a sequence, and it terminates usefully exactly when that sequence
  converges fast. [[Gradient Descent]] is the case that matters in [[MACHINE LEARNING]]
